title: What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture

body:
in Architecture, History |   	November 20th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Most of us remem­ber where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learn­ing that the most famous of all French cathe­drals had been bad­ly dam­aged rather than com­plete­ly destroyed, it still felt as if some­thing irre­place­able had been lost. It made no dif­fer­ence whether we’d actu­al­ly been to the place, as I had­n’t at the time. When I did final­ly make it to Paris four years lat­er, Notre-Dame’s restora­tion was still under­way, and con­struc­tion walls pre­vent­ed any­one from see­ing much of any­thing at ground lev­el, let alone enter­ing. Yet crowds still gath­ered to take pic­tures in the square out­side, appar­ent­ly find­ing that prox­im­i­ty to such a civ­i­liza­tion­al land­mark was enough, even in its par­tial­ly ruined and inac­ces­si­ble state.
Even with­out a chance to step inside, expe­ri­enc­ing Notre-Dame’s sur­round­ings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban con­text of Paris, cer­tain­ly deep­ens one’s under­stand­ing of the beau­ty of the cathe­dral itself. So does vis­it­ing oth­er, less wide­ly known exam­ples of the form, as shown by archi­tec­ture-and-his­to­ry YouTu­ber Manuel Bra­vo in his new video above.
Ordi­nary tourists in Paris may make a bee­line for Notre-Dame, but they’re hard­ly like­ly to find their way out to the oth­er medieval cathe­drals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glo­ri­ous in their own way, they’re per­haps even more valu­able in pro­vid­ing the con­text of Goth­ic church archi­tec­ture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.
As Bra­vo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade rep­re­sents “the moment in which Goth­ic façade achieves its most bal­anced syn­the­sis. The exper­i­ments and inno­va­tions of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, dis­ci­plined, and uni­fied into a com­po­si­tion in which no ele­ment appears arbi­trary or inde­pen­dent from the whole.” Among its most influ­en­tial appre­ci­a­tors was Vic­tor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Goth­ic archi­tec­ture was being demol­ished. His roman­tic evo­ca­tions of the medieval built envi­ron­ment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in Eng­lish, The Hunch­back of Notre-Dame) helped save the much dete­ri­o­rat­ed tit­u­lar struc­ture, which received an ambi­tious ren­o­va­tion under Eugène Vio­l­let-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond peri­od accu­ra­cy, adding such non-orig­i­nal details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain vis­i­ble dur­ing the lat­est restora­tion work. Vis­i­tors today may notice that the inte­ri­or does­n’t look exact­ly like it used to, but some will appre­ci­ate that even a mon­u­ment like Notre-Dame must change with the cen­turies.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Dramatic Waves Crash on Iceland's Coast in Photos by Vilhelm Gunnarsson
description:
All images © Vilhelm Gunnarsson, shared with permission
November 20, 2026


Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm
body:
All images © Vilhelm Gunnarsson, shared with permission
November 20, 2026


Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson, Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.
Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it. Explore a larger archive on Instagram.

title: Yoshitomo Nara's Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York
description: The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently vi
body:
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center, where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.
Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.
“Foggy Tale” (2026). Image courtesy of the artist, Equivalence Art Agency, and David Zwirner
In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.
Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery, 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.
Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.
Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake. The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t. 
Installation view of ‘Yoshitomo Nara’ at David Zwirner (2026)
In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb. 
As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”
The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.

title: 'We're Still Here' Celebrates Remarkable Quilts by 15 Contemporary Black Artists
description: In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangou
body:
In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising.
Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson—the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.
L’Merchie Frazier, “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here” (2026), nylon fiber; quilted, cotton-backed, 40 x 30 inches
For quilter Rosy Petri, Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery.
The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network (WCQN), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.
L’Merchie Frazier’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix—in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.
In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. 
Viola Burley Leak, “Maya Angelou II,” cotton, silk, metallic textiles; appliquéd and hand-painted quilt, 61 x 57 x 1 inches
“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”
We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release, Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers.

title: Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam's Embroideries in Green
description: Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the pas
body:
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.
Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness. Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.
The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram.

title: A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work
description: A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and V
body:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate. 
In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world. 



As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.
